LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) -- A former engineer for Rockwell International and Boeing was convicted Thursday of economic espionage and acting as an agent of China, authorities said. A Delta IV rocket launches on March 10, 2003 at Cape Canaveral, Florida. Dongfan "Greg" Chung, 73, was accused of stealing restricted technology and Boeing trade secrets, including information related to the space shuttle program and the Delta IV rocket. U.S. District Judge Cormac J. Carney convicted him on charges of conspiracy to commit economic espionage; six counts of economic espionage to benefit a foreign country; one count of acting as an agent of the People's Republic of China; and one count of making false statements to the FBI, according to a statement from federal prosecutors. Carney presided over Chung's three-week bench trial last month. In a bench trial, there is no jury and the judge decides whether to convict a defendant after hearing testimony. Chung was free on bond after his arrest by FBI agents and NASA investigators in February 2008. He was taken into custody after Carney's ruling was read. Chung, a native of China who is a naturalized United States citizen, was employed by Rockwell International from 1973 until Boeing acquired its defense and space unit in 1996, and by Boeing thereafter. He retired from Boeing in 2002, but returned as a contractor, a position he held until September 2006, prosecutors said. Chung held a "secret" security clearance, authorities said. "For years, Mr. Chung stole critical trade secrets from Boeing relating to the space shuttle and the Delta IV rocket -- all for the benefit of the government of China," said David Kris, assistant attorney general for national security, in the prosecutors' statement. "Today's verdict should serve as a warning to others willing to compromise America's economic and national security to assist foreign governments." The case against Chung resulted from an investigation into another engineer who obtained information for China. That engineer, Chi Mak, and several of his relatives were convicted of providing defense articles to the PRC, authorities said. Mak was sentenced to more than 24 years in prison last year. According to evidence presented at trial, individuals in the Chinese aviation industry began sending tasks to Chung via letter as early as 1979, federal prosecutors said. Over the years, the letters directed Chung to collect data related to the space shuttle and various military and civilian aircraft. In his letters back to China, Chung referenced materials he had already sent, including 24 manuals relating to the B-1 bomber, which Rockwell had forbidden for distribution outside the company and federal agencies. In addition, between 1985 and 2003, Chung traveled to China several times and met with government officials. His contacts in China discussed these trips in letters and recommended methods of passing information, authorities said. In a 2006 search of Chung's home, FBI and NASA agents found more than 250,000 pages of documents from Boeing, Rockwell and other defense contractors in the house and in its crawl space, prosecutors said. They included "scores of binders containing decades' worth of stress analysis reports, test results and design information for the space shuttle." Each economic espionage charge carries a maximum sentence of 15 years in prison and a $500,000 fine, authorities said. The charge of acting as an agent for a foreign government carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The charges of conspiracy to commit economic espionage and making false statements to federal investigators each carry a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. Chung is set for sentencing November 9.

In one of the most landmark insider-threat prosecutions in modern American history, former aerospace engineer Dongfan “Greg” Chung was convicted of economic espionage after abusing his high-level security clearance to steal state-of-the-art space shuttle and defense technologies for the Chinese government. Over a career spanning more than three decades at major U.S. defense contractors, Chung quietly siphoned off hundreds of thousands of pages of restricted research, handing Beijing the keys to advanced military and civilian aerospace developments. 

The case concluded with a severe federal conviction—a ruling that Department of Justice prosecutors hailed as a decisive line in the sand and a stern warning to anyone attempting to trade America’s national security and technological edge for foreign patronage.

---

### A Career Built on Trust and Access

Dongfan Chung, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in China, built an enviable career within the heart of the American defense industry. Starting in 1973, he worked as a stress analyst for Rockwell International, a primary contractor for NASA and the U.S. military. When Boeing acquired Rockwell’s defense and space divisions in 1996, Chung transitioned to the new company, retaining his access to critical projects.

Throughout his tenure, Chung held a high-level "Secret" security clearance. This clearance granted him unrestricted access to proprietary data detailing the inner workings of some of the nation’s most sensitive technological achievements, including NASA's Space Shuttle program, the C-17 Globemaster III military transport aircraft, the Delta IV rocket, and various satellite communication architectures. 

To his colleagues, Chung was a quiet, dedicated professional. Beneath that exterior, however, he was acting as a covert asset for the People's Republic of China (PRC).

---

### Decades of Theft: The Espionage Operation

Federal investigations later revealed that Chung’s espionage activities began as early as 1979—just six years after he joined Rockwell—and continued unabated until 2006. 

Chung was targeted and cultivated by officials from the state-owned Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC). Over the years, he received direct requests from Chinese officials asking for specific technical documentation. In response, Chung methodically gathered, organized, and passed along manuals, schematics, design details, and operational data.

His primary targets included:
*   **The Space Shuttle Program:** Detailed technical specs regarding the shuttle's main engine and thermal protection tiles.
*   **Military Transport:** Highly restricted design data for the C-17 Globemaster III aircraft.
*   **Rocketry:** Proprietary engineering data for the Delta IV launch vehicle, used to lift critical military and intelligence satellites into orbit.

Chung communicated with his handlers via hidden correspondence and traveled to China under the guise of giving technical lectures. In letters seized by federal agents, Chung openly declared his desire to contribute to the "motherland," writing that he wanted to help China modernize its aerospace capabilities.

---

### Unraveling the Plot

The unraveling of Chung’s multi-decade spy ring came as a byproduct of another high-profile espionage investigation. In 2005, federal agents arresting Chi Mak—an engineer who was also passing military secrets to China—discovered evidence pointing toward a second mole operating inside Southern California's defense sector.

In September 2006, FBI and federal law enforcement agents executed a search warrant on Chung’s home in Orange, California. What they discovered was staggering: hidden beneath his house, inside his garage, and tucked into his closet were over 300,000 pages of restricted engineering documents, proprietary corporate manuals, and sensitive government research papers. 

Federal prosecutors formally charged Chung in 2008 with economic espionage, conspiracy to commit economic espionage, acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government, and making false statements to federal investigators.

---

### The Verdict and Legacy: A Warning to Insiders

In 2009, following a bench trial, U.S. District Judge Cormac J. Carney found the 73-year-old Chung guilty on six counts of economic espionage, among other federal charges. In February 2010, Judge Carney sentenced Chung to 15 years and eight months in federal prison—effectively a life sentence given the defendant's age.

The trial was historically significant: it marked the very first bench trial conviction under the Economic Espionage Act of 1996, setting a vital legal precedent for how the U.S. government prosecutes state-sponsored corporate theft.

Following the trial, federal prosecutors emphasized the broader national security implications of the ruling. Department of Justice officials framed the verdict as a stark warning to corporate employees, researchers, and government clearance holders nationwide: compromise America’s economic and national security for a foreign power, and you will face severe federal justice.

The conviction of Greg Chung served as a wake-up call for the defense industry, highlighting the vulnerability of critical technology to "insider threats" and reshaping how defense contractors protect proprietary research in an era of intense geopolitical competition.

Dongfan "Greg" Chung, 73, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in China, was convicted of acting as an unregistered foreign agent, economic espionage, trade secret theft, and making false statements to federal agents. 

The ruling marks the first time a defendant has been convicted of economic espionage in a bench trial since the Economic Espionage Act was passed by Congress in 1996.

U.S. District Judge Cormac J. Carney delivered the verdict in a Santa Ana court following a bench trial, concluding that Chung betrayed his adopted country out of a desire to assist his homeland. 

"Mr. Chung sacrificed the security of his country for the glory of the People's Republic of China," Judge Carney said during the ruling.

### Decades of Secrets Hidden Underneath a House

Federal prosecutors revealed a staggering trove of classified and proprietary information uncovered during a search of Chung’s Orange, California, home in 2006. 

Agents found more than 300,000 pages of sensitive documents stashed in his home, hidden inside boxes under his house and in a crawlspace. The stolen materials detailed critical military and aerospace technologies, including:

*   The Space Shuttle's thermal protection system
*   The C-17 Globemaster III military transport aircraft
*   The Delta IV rocket booster system
*   Naval military technology, including harbor-defense systems

According to court evidence, Chung’s espionage activities began as early as the late 1970s while he was employed by Rockwell International, an aerospace giant whose defense and space divisions were later acquired by Boeing in 1996. 

Letters presented by prosecutors showed that officials from China’s aviation industry systematically directed Chung to collect specific military technology. In one 1979 letter, Chinese officials asked Chung for technical data, encouraging him to serve "the motherland." 

Chung complied, traveling to China under the guise of giving lectures while secretly meeting with Chinese intelligence agents to deliver documents, prosecutors said.

### A Calculated Betrayal

"This was not an isolated incident, but a decades-long campaign to funnel sensitive American technological innovations directly to a foreign power," said Assistant Attorney General for National Security David Kris in a statement following the verdict. "Today's conviction brings to justice an individual who put American national security at risk for personal and ideological loyalty to another nation."

Chung’s defense team argued that the retired engineer was merely an avid researcher and a "pack rat" who brought work home to study, claiming he never intended to harm the United States. 

However, federal prosecutors systematically dismantled that defense, pointing to covert communications, organized travel itineraries, and detailed logs kept by Chung that cataloged the exact technical manuals he was gathering for Beijing.

### FBI Unraveled Network

The investigation into Chung grew out of a separate high-profile espionage probe involving Chi Mak, a defense contractor engineer convicted in 2007 of conspiring to export sensitive U.S. military technology to China. 

While searching Mak’s home, FBI agents uncovered documents that pointed directly to Chung, prompting a years-long federal probe that ultimately dismantled Chung's operation.

U.S. counterintelligence officials have long warned that foreign entities, particularly China, actively target current and former defense contractors to acquire advanced technology without the cost of independent research and development.

Chung faces a maximum statutory sentence of more than 100 years in federal prison when he is sentenced later this year. He remains in federal custody.

# Inside the FBI Sting That Exposed China’s Billion-Dollar Jet Engine Heist

**By Marcus Vance**  
*National Security & Aerospace Correspondent*  
**WASHINGTON** — In what federal prosecutors have described as a blueprint for state-sponsored economic warfare, a unprecedented counterintelligence operation exposed a decade-long effort by Chinese intelligence officers to steal America’s most closely guarded aerospace secrets.

The case of *United States v. Xu Yanjun*—which culminated in a landmark 20-year federal prison sentence—marked the first time in history that a operative from China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS) was lured out of hiding, extradited to the United States, and convicted by a federal jury. 

At the center of the espionage campaign was a prize worth billions in research and development: the proprietary design and manufacturing processes for GE Aviation’s carbon-fiber composite jet engine fan blades—a technology possessed by only a handful of companies worldwide.

---

### The Target: Unlocking the Holy Grail of Aviation

For decades, Western aerospace giants like GE Aviation (now GE Aerospace) and Pratt & Whitney held a virtual monopoly on advanced jet engine propulsion. While China successfully built commercial airframes, such as the COMAC C919, its domestic defense and aviation sectors remained hobbled by a crucial vulnerability: an inability to manufacture reliable, lightweight, heat-resistant jet engines.

The "holy grail" of modern commercial aviation engines is the composite fan blade. Made from ultra-thin layers of carbon fiber bonded with proprietary resins and edged with titanium, these blades allow engines like the CFM LEAP and GE90 to operate at extreme temperatures and pressures while dramatically reducing fuel consumption.

Developing this single component required GE to spend over 30 years and billions of dollars in iterative engineering.

For the Jiangsu State Security Department (JSSD)—a regional arm of China’s top intelligence agency, the MSS—spending decades on R&D was unnecessary. Intelligence officials calculated that stealing the design specifications, thermal barrier coatings, and containment testing data would allow Chinese state-owned enterprises, particularly the Aero Engine Corporation of China (AECC), to skip generations of trial-and-error engineering.

```
       [ Chinese MSS / JSSD Operatives ]
                      │
   ┌──────────────────┴──────────────────┐
   ▼                                     ▼
[ Front Academic Orgs ]       [ Covert Hackers / Cyber ]
 (Nanjing University)              (Spear-phishing)
   │                                     │
   └──────────────────┬──────────────────┘
                      ▼
         [ Target: US Aerospace Engineers ]
                      │
                      ▼
        [ Exfiltration of IP / Specs ]
```

---

### The Anatomy of an Infiltration

According to federal court documents and evidence presented at trial, Xu Yanjun, who operated under the alias "Qu Hui," served as a deputy division director within the JSSD. His primary mandate was systemic intellectual property theft targeting Western aerospace firms, including GE Aviation, Honeywell, and Safran.

Xu’s playbook relied on a sophisticated mix of academic baiting, social engineering, and cyber-exploitation:

1. **The Academic Cover:** Xu utilized front organizations, primarily the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics (NUAA), one of China's premier military-linked universities. 
2. **The Lure:** Using LinkedIn and industry registries, Xu identified current and former high-level aerospace engineers holding security clearances. Targets were invited to China under the guise of delivering "guest lectures" or participating in academic exchanges, with all travel expenses paid alongside generous honorariums.
3. **The Extraction:** Once the engineers arrived in China, Xu and his team entertained them at lavish dinners before placing malware-infected thumb drives into their personal devices or hosting presentations in rooms where laptops were secretly accessed and mirrored.

In 2017, Xu set his sights on an elite structural engineer working at GE Aviation’s headquarters in Evendale, Ohio. 

---

### The Sting in Brussels

The GE engineer, whose identity was protected in court documents under the pseudonym "Employee Five," was invited to present a paper at NUAA. During a trip to Nanjing, the engineer was introduced to Xu. Over dinner, Xu subtly shifted the conversation from general university lectures to highly specific, proprietary mathematical models used to test blade containment during catastrophic engine failures.

Recognizing that Xu was asking for trade secrets, the engineer reported the interaction to GE’s corporate security team upon returning to Ohio, who immediately alerted the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Working alongside federal agents, the engineer agreed to act as an undercover asset. For months, under FBI supervision, the engineer maintained encrypted communications via WeChat with Xu, dangling controlled fragments of technical data.

Convinced he was close to securing the complete design system for GE's composite engine blades, Xu requested an in-person meeting in Europe to receive system diagnostic files directly onto a portable hard drive.

In April 2018, Xu flew to Brussels, Belgium, believing he was meeting the GE engineer in a hotel cafe. Instead, he was arrested by Belgian federal police acting on a secret arrest warrant issued by the U.S. District Court in Cincinnati.

Following a six-month legal battle over extradition, Xu was flown to the United States in October 2018 to face federal economic espionage charges—a major intelligence coup for the U.S. Department of Justice.

---

### Trial and Forensics: A Mountain of Digital Evidence

The trial, held in Cincinnati in late 2021, exposed the internal operations of China's state intelligence apparatus. 

FBI cyber-forensic analysts who examined Xu’s seized iPhone and encrypted cloud accounts presented devastating evidence to the jury. Among the files recovered were:
* Internal MSS administrative memos listing specific aerospace technologies targeted for theft.
* Direct communications between Xu and officials at state-owned Chinese military suppliers detailing lists of technical questions to ask U.S. engineers.
* A handwritten note recovered from Xu’s personal belongings that contained an eerie assessment of his work: *"Obtain the design specs... system testing is the hardest part. Save time, save money."*
